aiOverview.content: On March 29, 2026, professional golfer Gary Woodland achieved a remarkable comeback victory at the Houston Open, his first PGA Tour win since the 2019 U.S. Open and his first since undergoing surgery to remove a benign brain tumor. Brain Tumor and Surgery (2023) Diagnosis: In May 2023, an MRI revealed a lesion on Woodland's brain, which was causing severe symptoms including fear, anxiety, and partial seizures. Surgery: On September 18, 2023, Woodland underwent a craniotomy to remove the tumor. Result: Doctors were able to remove the majority of the tumor, which was determined to be benign. However, a small portion of the tumor remains, as it was too close to critical areas (near the amygdala, affecting fear/anxiety, and the optic tract) to safely remove. Return: Just four months later, in January 2024, Woodland returned to competitive golf at the Sony Open. Post-Surgery Challenges and Recovery (2025–2026) PTSD Diagnosis: In early 2026, Woodland revealed he had been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) about a year prior, leading to significant mental and emotional struggles after the operation. Symptoms: He described experiencing intense fear, anxiety, and "hypervigilance" on the golf course, particularly when people were behind him. Resilience: Despite these challenges, and a 2025 diagnosis revealing the need to manage the remaining tumor, Woodland continued to play. 2026 Victory: Following his public disclosure of his PTSD battle, which he said lifted a massive weight off his shoulders, he secured his fifth PGA Tour win at the Houston Open in March 2026. Woodland was honored with the PGA Tour Courage Award in February 2025 for his journey.
